summary: Describes how to carry XML-RPC messages, in which a client asks a server to run a procedure and return a result, over BEEP instead of HTTP. It defines the mapping onto a BEEP profile. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: XML-RPC lets one computer ask another to do a job and send back the answer. Usually the notes travel by web. This memo shows how to send them by another delivery service called BEEP.

questions: how does xml-rpc work without http
what port does xml-rpc over beep use
what is the xmlrpc.beeps url scheme
subtitle: How to carry XML-RPC procedure calls over BEEP channels instead of HTTP.

tldr.problem: XML-RPC messages are defined for transfer over HTTP, but some deployments want to send them over the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP).
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a BEEP profile for XML-RPC. A short boot exchange picks the resource, then each XML-RPC request goes in a MSG and each response comes back in a RPY. It also defines two URL schemes, xmlrpc.beep and xmlrpc.beeps.
tldr.outcome: XML-RPC can run over BEEP over TCP, with optional privacy tuning. This is an Experimental memo and it is updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 3529 is an Experimental memo and it is updated by RFC 8553. The text itself does not describe any deployments.

sections.title: XML-RPC Carried Over BEEP
sections.content:
XML-RPC defines an XML format for messages sent between clients and servers. A message holds either a procedure to run with its parameters, or the result of running it. Parameters and results can be scalars, numbers, strings, dates, or complex record and list structures.

The abstract says XML-RPC uses HTTP. This memo specifies how to use the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) to transfer the same messages instead. The words "request" and "response" mean the methodCall and methodResponse elements from the XML-RPC specification.
sections.eli5: The same questions and answers are used as before. Only the delivery truck changes, from the web to BEEP.

sections.title: The BEEP Profile and Its Boot Exchange
sections.content:
The profile is identified by http://iana.org/beep/transient/xmlrpc in the profile element when a channel is created. The serverName attribute of the start element names the virtual host of the server peer, much like the HTTP Host header.

The profile has two states. In boot, the initial state, the peer that asked for the channel sends a bootmsg with a mandatory resource attribute, which is like the path of an HTTP request. If the other peer recognizes the resource it answers bootrpy and the channel moves to ready. Otherwise it sends an error and the channel stays in boot, even though the channel was created.

In ready, the initiator sends a MSG containing a request and the other peer completes the exchange with a RPY containing the response. Normally the boot message and its reply travel inside channel creation.
sections.eli5: First the caller says which service it wants, like asking for a department on the phone. If the department exists, calls can begin. If not, the caller has to try again.

sections.title: Message Packages and Exchange
sections.content:
Requests and responses are encoded as UTF-8 and sent with the media type application/xml. The RFC shows an examples.getStateName call with the integer parameter 41 answered by the string South Dakota.

Each call is a one-to-one exchange: the client sends one MSG with a request and the server sends back one RPY with a response. The profile does not use ERR for XML-RPC faults in one-to-one exchanges. Whatever response the server generates always goes in the RPY.
sections.eli5: One question goes in one envelope and one answer comes back in one envelope. Even a failed call is answered in the normal answer envelope.

sections.title: URL Schemes and Address Lookup
sections.content:
Two schemes identify XML-RPC over BEEP over TCP: xmlrpc.beep and xmlrpc.beeps. Both use generic URI syntax, with the path mapped to the boot message's resource (defaulting to /). Scheme and authority are case-insensitive.

For address lookup, a domain name with a port gets A records looked up and the port used directly. A domain name with no port uses the SRV algorithm with service xmlrpc-beep and protocol tcp. If no suitable SRV records exist, A records are used with the port IANA assigned in section 6.4. An IP address in the authority is used directly with no DNS query, taking the port if present and otherwise the assigned port.

The xmlrpc.beeps scheme is identical except that the BEEP session must first be tuned for privacy, either by a transport security profile or by a user authentication profile that supports transport security. The client must put the URL authority in the serverName attribute of that tuning start. When TLS is used, the client must verify that the authority matches the server's identity in its certificate.
sections.eli5: The web address says where to go and which door to knock on. The version with the extra s first puts the conversation in a locked room and checks the host is who it says it is.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Service provisioning is a policy matter, but at a minimum all implementations must provide these tuning profiles: http://iana.org/beep/SASL/DIGEST-MD5 for authentication, http://iana.org/beep/TLS using the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher for confidentiality, and the same TLS profile with client-side certificates for both.

Implementations may also offer MIME-based security for message integrity and confidentiality, such as OpenPGP or S/MIME. For BEEP-specific issues the memo points to section 9 of the BEEP core specification, RFC 3080.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to support at least one way to prove who they are and one way to keep the messages secret.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The memo registers the XML-RPC profile, the xmlrpc.beep and xmlrpc.beeps URL schemes, and a well-known TCP port with the short name xmlrpc-beep. Appendix B records that IANA registered port 602 for it.

The profile registration lists bootmsg and methodCall as messages starting one-to-one exchanges, and bootrpy and methodResponse as positive replies. Negative replies use error, and there are no one-to-many exchanges.
sections.eli5: The memo gets an official name tag, a web-style prefix and a numbered door, so everyone uses the same ones.

messages.label: RPY: methodResponse
messages.note: The response, even for an XML-RPC fault.
